title: MCP Tasks (async): Why Aren't Any Agents Supporting Them? — Cornelia Davis, Temporal

primary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 77%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: MCP is a developer-facing protocol specification used by software builders integrating tools with AI agents. The talk targets developers implementing MCP task support in clients and servers.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The demonstrated use case is an enterprise back-office workflow: purchase order processing, invoice validation against an ERP, and human approval steps — classic enterprise operations automation.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The MCP tasks protocol itself is cross-domain and not tied to a specific application vertical; the invoice demo is just one example of a broader pattern.

summary: Cornelia Davis, Developer Advocate at Temporal Technologies, presents a detailed analysis of the MCP (Model Context Protocol) tasks specification — the mechanism for long-running, asynchronous tool calls that return a handle instead of an immediate response. She explains why almost no AI agents currently support MCP tasks: the November 2025 V1 spec is experimental and marked by awkward stateful patterns, while a radically redesigned V2 arrived in July 2026. Davis grounds the talk in a purchase order and invoice processing workflow that exercises the full task lifecycle: working, input_required, completed, cancelled, and failed. She demonstrates a FastMCP-based client and server, showing durability in practice — a task survives even when MCP servers are not yet running. She identifies two critical V1 problems: tasks/list has no filtering and fails at scale with millions of tasks, and tasks/result tunnels input_required over a fragile long-running connection that is hard to resume after disconnection. The V1 client protocol handler is so complex that no existing MCP clients implement tasks at all. V2 addresses these issues by moving to a stateless core with tasks as a structured extension (SEP-2663), removing tasks/list entirely, and replacing long-running input_required sessions with a client-driven tasks/update endpoint analogous to Temporal's signal mechanism. Life cycle management remains unchanged from V1. Davis notes remaining scalability challenges — a million tasks still means a million clients polling via tasks/get — but a notifications protocol (subscriptions/listen) shows promise. She plans to implement V2 task support in FastMCP within one to two months and shares a Git repository with slides and code.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a cohesive narrative about the evolution of AI agent infrastructure from simple synchronous tool calls to durable, asynchronous, human-in-the-loop workflows. The MCP tasks specification (both V1 and V2) is the protocol-level enabler, while stateless protocol design, durable execution, and the client-driven update endpoint are the architectural principles that make it practical at scale. The task lifecycle state machine and polling-based retrieval define the operational contract between agents and tools. FastMCP provides the implementation framework that bridges specification and practice. Human-in-the-loop workflows and fault tolerance represent the real-world requirements driving this evolution. Finally, the scalability challenges and notifications protocol point to the remaining work needed for enterprise-grade adoption. Together, these concepts trace the full path from protocol design through implementation to production deployment of long-running AI agent tasks.
temporalContext: The video was published on August 2, 2026, and the V2 MCP specification (2026-07-28) had been officially released just five days prior on July 28, 2026. The V1 tasks spec shipped experimentally in November 2025 (version 2025-11-25). Angie Jones announced the stateless protocol direction in May 2026. Davis presented an earlier version of this material at the MCP Dev Summit NA in March 2026. The research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. At the time of the talk, V2 was brand-new, Davis was planning to implement V2 task support in FastMCP within one to two months, and no off-the-shelf MCP clients yet supported tasks. The V1.x SDKs have a bug-fix support window of at least six months post-V2 release. MCP has surpassed 400M monthly SDK downloads and is now governed under the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation).
takeaways: MCP tasks let a tool run long, return a handle, report progress, pause for human input, and survive disconnections rather than answering in one request-response call
The November V1 spec is experimental, complex, and largely unimplemented by agents; V2 with radical changes arrives in July
V2 introduces a stateless core with tasks as an extension, removing tasklist and replacing long-running connections with a client-driven update endpoint
V1 tasklist has no filter and fails at scale with millions of tasks; V1 input-required tunnels over a fragile long-running connection
Durability is mandatory: once a task is launched it cannot disappear and must survive client, server, and network failures
V1 client protocol implementation is extremely involved, which is why no existing MCP clients support tasks
V2 life cycle management is unchanged from V1, but clients should persist task IDs since there is no way to recover them otherwise
Even V2 has scaling challenges: million-task workloads still require per-task polling, though a notifications protocol shows promise
Davis is building a Fast MCP implementation of V2 task support expected within one to two months
Server-side durability was covered in her March MCP Dev Summit talk; this session focuses on the client side

concepts.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
concepts.explanation: MCP is an open protocol standard (originated by Anthropic, now under the Agentic AI Foundation within the Linux Foundation) for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources. The tasks extension specifically enables long-running, asynchronous tool calls that go beyond simple request-response.
concepts.importance: MCP is the foundational protocol ecosystem that the entire talk analyzes. It is becoming the standard interface between AI agents and tools, with over 400M monthly SDK downloads, making its task specification critical for the next generation of agent capabilities.

concepts.name: AI Agent Tool Integration with Long-Running Operations
concepts.explanation: Current AI agent tool calls are synchronous request-response. MCP tasks extend this model to support long-running operations where a tool may take minutes, hours, or days, requiring the agent to track task handles and poll for results rather than blocking on a single call.
concepts.importance: This represents the evolution from simple tool calls to production-grade agent workflows. Without long-running task support, agents are limited to operations that complete within a single request, constraining real-world utility for enterprise workflows like invoice processing.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop AI Workflows
concepts.explanation: MCP tasks support an input_required state where a running task pauses to request human input — such as approving an invoice before payment. V2's client-driven tasks/update endpoint enables this without holding a long-lived connection open during the human deliberation period.
concepts.importance: Human-in-the-loop is essential for enterprise AI adoption where automated decisions require oversight. The protocol's ability to pause, wait for human input, and resume is what makes it suitable for regulated business processes.

concepts.name: Agent Infrastructure Fault Tolerance
concepts.explanation: The durability mandate for MCP tasks means that agent infrastructure must survive client crashes, server failures, and network disconnections. This aligns with Temporal's durable execution paradigm where workflow state is captured at every step and recovered automatically.
concepts.importance: As AI agents move from demos to production, fault tolerance becomes non-negotiable. The talk bridges AI agent infrastructure with proven distributed systems reliability patterns, making it relevant for building production-grade agent platforms.

concepts.name: AI Agent Scalability Challenges
concepts.explanation: Even with V2's improvements, scaling to millions of concurrent tasks remains challenging because each task requires a separate client polling via tasks/get. A notifications protocol (subscriptions/listen) is proposed to address this by allowing servers to push status updates instead of clients polling.
concepts.importance: Scalability determines whether MCP tasks can support enterprise-scale deployments with thousands or millions of concurrent long-running operations. Understanding these limits and the proposed solutions is critical for architects designing large-scale agent platforms.

concepts.name: MCP Tasks Specification (V1 and V2)
concepts.explanation: The MCP tasks protocol defines how tools can run long, return a task handle instead of a direct response, report progress, pause for human input, and survive disconnections. V1 (2025-11-25) is experimental with stateful patterns; V2 (2026-07-28, SEP-2663) introduces a stateless core with tasks as a structured extension, removing tasks/list and replacing long-running connections with a client-driven tasks/update endpoint.
concepts.importance: This is the central subject of the talk. Understanding the protocol evolution from V1 to V2 is essential for developers building MCP-compatible agents and tool servers that handle asynchronous, long-running operations.

concepts.name: Stateless vs Stateful Protocol Design
concepts.explanation: V1 MCP tasks relied on stateful patterns — long-running connections for input_required and a stateful tasks/list endpoint. V2 moves to a stateless core where each request is independent, which Davis considers critical for large-scale distributed systems, drawing on her microservices experience that stateful protocols are the worst thing at scale.
concepts.importance: The stateless-vs-stateful tradeoff is the core architectural decision driving the V2 redesign. It determines whether MCP task infrastructure can scale on ordinary HTTP infrastructure (serverless, edge) or requires persistent session management.

concepts.name: Durable Execution for Long-Running Tasks
concepts.explanation: The MCP tasks spec mandates durability: once a task is launched it cannot disappear and must survive client crashes, server failures, and network disconnections. Davis draws on Temporal's durable execution paradigm to illustrate this requirement and demonstrates it by showing a task persisting even before MCP servers were running.
concepts.importance: Durability is the fundamental property that distinguishes tasks from synchronous tool calls. Without it, long-running operations would be lost on any infrastructure blip, making tasks unusable for real-world workflows like invoice processing with human approval delays.

concepts.name: Client-Driven Update Endpoint (Signal Pattern)
concepts.explanation: V2 replaces V1's long-running connection for input_required with a client-driven tasks/update endpoint, where the client sends updates to the server at its own discretion. Davis explicitly analogizes this to Temporal's signal mechanism, where external inputs are delivered to a running workflow asynchronously.
concepts.importance: This is the key V2 innovation that eliminates the fragile long-running connection problem. It shifts control from server-pushed elicitation to client-driven updates, making the protocol resilient to disconnections and much simpler to implement.

concepts.name: Task Lifecycle State Machine
concepts.explanation: Both V1 and V2 define a task lifecycle with states: working, input_required, completed, cancelled, and failed. A task can transition from working to input_required and back to working before reaching a terminal state. This state machine is unchanged between V1 and V2.
concepts.importance: The lifecycle states define the contract between clients and servers for managing long-running tasks. Understanding these states is prerequisite for implementing correct task tracking, human-in-the-loop approval, and error handling.

concepts.name: Polling-Based Task Status Retrieval
concepts.explanation: V2 replaces V1's blocking tasks/result with polling via tasks/get. Clients periodically query the server for task status and results. At scale (millions of tasks), this creates a polling overhead problem that the notifications protocol (subscriptions/listen) aims to address.
concepts.importance: Polling is the V2 mechanism for task status tracking, replacing V1's blocking approach. Understanding its tradeoffs is essential for building scalable MCP task infrastructure and knowing when to use notifications instead.

concepts.name: Protocol Extension Mechanism
concepts.explanation: V2 introduces a structured extensions framework where features like tasks are versioned extensions with namespaced identifiers (e.g., io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks) rather than being baked into the core protocol. This allows independent versioning and optional adoption.
concepts.importance: The extension mechanism is the structural change that enables tasks to evolve independently of the core protocol, supporting a 12-month deprecation window and allowing clients and servers to negotiate capabilities.

concepts.name: FastMCP Framework for MCP Implementation
concepts.explanation: FastMCP is a Python MCP application framework maintained by PrefectHQ that supports building MCP servers, clients, and interactive apps. Davis uses it for her client implementation and plans to extend it with V2 task support. It currently implements the V1 background task protocol (SEP-1686).
concepts.importance: FastMCP is the practical implementation vehicle for the talk's concepts. It represents the tooling layer that developers will use to build MCP task-capable clients and servers, making the specification actionable.

sections.title: Introduction and why agents avoid MCP tasks
sections.summary: Davis introduces the talk title, notes the November MCP tasks spec is experimental, and previews that agents are smart to wait because V2 brings radical changes in July. She gives her background: technologist at Temporal, distributed systems veteran, author of a cloud native patterns book.

sections.title: Concrete use case: purchase order and invoice processing
sections.summary: A purchase order workflow records goods received, runs parallel back-office steps, and pays invoices via a long-running MCP tool. The invoice tool validates against an ERP, waits for human approval, reconciles, and loops. Davis shows code snippets highlighting a signal mechanism for asynchronous interaction.

sections.title: MCP tasks overview and durability requirement
sections.summary: A simple sequence diagram shows invoking a tool and getting back a handle. Over long horizons, network blips, crashes, and human delays threaten tasks. The spec mandates durability: tasks cannot disappear and must survive client, server, and connection failures. She references her March MCP Dev Summit talk for server-side details.

sections.title: Demo: invoice processing dashboard
sections.summary: Davis demonstrates a dashboard submitting a purchase order, tracking invoice task state through submitted, working, input required, and completed. She starts backend (MCP server) and frontend (Fast MCP client) in separate windows, shows the task persisted even before servers were running, approves a human input step, and observes the backend continue with retries and completion.

sections.title: Tasks V1: life cycle and tool semantics
sections.summary: V1 defines a task life cycle of working, input required, complete, canceled, or failed. Tool semantics include tools/call with async metadata, task get/cancel/list, and task/result. The top four operations are request-response; the bottom keeps a connection alive. Two major challenges emerge: tasklist implies a stateful protocol, and the server is responsible for durability through a stateful endpoint.

sections.title: V1 challenges: tasklist scale and task result complexity
sections.summary: Davis explains tasklist works for a few tasks but fails at scale with a million tasks since there is no filter. Task result tunnels input required over a long-running connection that is tricky to resume after disconnection. She shows the V1 client protocol handler architecture using Fast MCP, emphasizing the complexity that explains why no clients implement tasks.

sections.title: V2: stateless core and extensions
sections.summary: Angie Jones announced in May that the V2 protocol is going stateless, which Davis celebrates. V2 has a stateless core with structured MCP extensions; tasks become an extension. Tasklist is removed. Input required over a long session is replaced by a client-driven update endpoint like Temporal's signal. Task result stays but loses the long-session protocol. Life cycle management is unchanged. Clients should persist task IDs, though the spec oddly uses should rather than MUST.

sections.title: Second demo and implementation roadmap
sections.summary: Davis shows a second demo with multiple POs in flight, noting the V1 reference implementation handled input-required as FIFO. She shows the task tracker implementing the V1 protocol as a workflow. V2 client-server protocol is much cleaner. She summarizes implementation requirements, shares a Git repo with slides, notes remaining scale challenges (million-task polling), previews a notifications protocol, and plans a Fast MCP V2 implementation within one to two months.

organization.name: Model Context Protocol
organization.summary: Open-source protocol specification for connecting AI applications to external systems, tools, and data sources. Originally created by Anthropic in November 2024 and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation on December 9, 2025. The MCP Tasks specification (V1 2025-11-25 experimental, V2 2026-07-28 official extension SEP-2663) is the primary subject of this video. The protocol has over 10,000 published MCP servers and is adopted by Claude, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, VS Code, and ChatGPT.

technologies.label: MCP Tasks Specification (V1 Experimental and V2 Extension)
technologies.summary: The MCP Tasks Specification is the central technology of the video. It defines how AI agent tool calls can be long-running and asynchronous: a tool returns a task handle instead of an immediate result, the task reports progress, can pause for human input, and must survive infrastructure failures. V1 (2025-11-25, SEP-1686) shipped experimentally in the core protocol with stateful patterns — an unfiltered tasks/list endpoint that fails at scale and a blocking tasks/result that tunnels input_required over a fragile long-running connection. V2 (2026-07-28, SEP-2663) radically redesigns tasks as a structured extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks): stateless core, tasks/list removed, blocking tasks/result replaced by polling tasks/get, and a new client-driven tasks/update endpoint for human input. The task lifecycle state machine (working, input_required, completed, cancelled, failed) is unchanged. No off-the-shelf MCP clients currently support tasks due to V1's implementation complexity.
technologies.role: This is the primary subject of the entire talk. Davis analyzes the V1 spec's design problems, previews the V2 redesign, and demonstrates both versions using a purchase order and invoice processing workflow.

technologies.label: MCP Stateless Core Architecture and Extension Framework
technologies.summary: The MCP Stateless Core Architecture is the foundational architectural shift in V2 that enables tasks and other features to scale on ordinary HTTP infrastructure (serverless, edge). V1's stateful protocol required long-running connections and session management, which Davis identifies as fundamentally unsuitable for large-scale distributed systems. V2's stateless core makes each request independent, introduces a structured extension framework with namespaced identifiers and capability negotiation, and replaces V1's blocking operations with polling and client-driven updates. The notifications protocol (subscriptions/listen) is proposed to address remaining polling overhead at million-task scale.
technologies.role: The stateless-vs-stateful tradeoff is the core architectural argument of the talk. Davis celebrates the V2 stateless shift, explains the extension mechanism, and highlights remaining scalability challenges with the notifications protocol as a future solution.

technologies.label: Temporal Durable Execution Platform
technologies.summary: Temporal provides an open-source durable execution platform where workflows capture state at every step and automatically recover from infrastructure failures. The MCP tasks specification mandates this same durability: once launched, a task cannot disappear and must survive client crashes, server failures, and network disconnections. Davis uses Temporal as both the implementation vehicle for her demo and the conceptual model for understanding MCP task durability. The V2 tasks/update endpoint is explicitly analogized to Temporal's signal mechanism, where external inputs are delivered asynchronously to running workflows.
technologies.role: Temporal is the speaker's employer and the technology powering the demo. The durable execution paradigm is the lens through which Davis analyzes MCP task requirements, and the signal mechanism is the analogy for V2's tasks/update endpoint.

technologies.label: FastMCP Python Framework
technologies.summary: FastMCP is a full-featured Python MCP application framework maintained by PrefectHQ for building MCP servers, clients, and interactive apps. It provides a higher-level, Pythonic abstraction over the official MCP Python SDK. Davis uses FastMCP for her client implementation in the demo and plans to implement V2 task support (SEP-2663) within one to two months. The framework currently implements the V1 background task protocol (SEP-1686) with task=True decorators, TaskConfig modes, and client-side Task/ToolTask classes. Its task system is powered by Docket, originally built by Prefect. FastMCP represents the practical tooling layer that makes the MCP tasks specification actionable for developers.
technologies.role: FastMCP is the implementation framework for both the demo (client and server) and the planned V2 task support. Davis explicitly states she uses FastMCP on the client side and intends to implement V2 task support in it, making it the bridge between specification and practice.

Implement a V2 task client that manages 100 concurrent tasks via polling and measure polling overhead; then prototype a subscriptions/listen notifications approach and compare scalability characteristics

Migrate a V1-style tasks/list + tasks/result implementation to V2 by replacing blocking calls with tasks/get polling, removing tasks/list usage, and switching from long-running input_required sessions to client-driven tasks/update — documenting each breaking change encountered
